notes: The status panel shrinks to the walking bar whenever a screen is open over the map. Its readouts answer “how am I doing while walking”, and with a panel open you are reading the panel — the numbers were just height taken off what you came to read. The buttons stay, because switching screens is the one thing still wanted.

Groundwork for hand-drawn maps. Terrain and finds can now be set one hex at a time from a file, and a hand-drawn hex beats every guess the game makes — the tile reading and the hash both — because a person looked at that hex and said so.
The editor that draws those files paints straight onto the live map rather than onto a screenshot: real tiles, real hexes, exact coordinates, nothing to line up.

The Fuming Lake can be walked wherever you live. Every place in the tale was a fixed coordinate in one Tampere park, and beginning it means standing on the statue — so anybody who lives anywhere else could not begin it at all. The walk keeps its exact shape; it now starts at your own Hearth.
If the tale sits oddly on your ground — a lake on dry land, a bridge with no stream — that is worth saying. Matching the story to real places is what the map editor is for.

There is a fishing village at Härmälänranta. Nineteen hexes of it, held for good — it does not rot, and walking on it takes nothing. It is the first thing on this map that is *there* rather than generated around wherever you happen to start.

Its quay trades. Twenty of one resource for fifteen of another, and the quarter they keep is the whole reason it is a choice rather than a button you press in a loop: swapping back and forth leaves you with less than you started.
Diplomacy happens at one hex, so reaching a city state is a walk to a place. Every other hex of the village tells you how far its quay is, so the door is not a hunt.
Ground now says what it is for, even when you cannot build it yet. A mountain lists the Mine and the Quarry with “Needs Mining” beside them, instead of reading as ground with nothing to offer.

The Mine has existed for a long time. It was filed alphabetically behind a “+ 14 more” toggle among fourteen buildings that could never stand on a mountain, so nobody ever found it. Only buildings for other ground are hidden now, and the toggle says so.

Some ground has something on it. About one hex in eight carries a find — Wheat, a Herd, Deer, Furs, Gems, Marble, Fish, Amber or Spices — and it belongs to its own terrain: fish in water, gems in mountains, wheat on the plain. It adds to what that hex pays every hour, roughly doubling it.
It is the plain that needed this most. Two thirds of the map is plain and plain yields nothing, so most ground was interchangeable; now some of it is worth walking to.

A find pays only once you have revealed the hex, which turns revealing from a one-off bonus into the way you learn what your own land is worth. Your lands lists every find you have made, and an unrevealed hex keeps its own secret.
Where a find is, is fixed — never rolled. Two players on the same street find the same deer, and reloading the page does not shuffle them.

New page: Your lands, from the ☰ menu. Every hex you hold, with its ground, what it yields, its strength, the days you have walked it, the Work standing on it, and how long before the Void takes it back.

Unrevealed ground is listed first, because revealing is free, pays every time, and is the only thing on the list you can act on without walking anywhere. After that comes whatever is closest to being lost; ground that cannot be lost sinks to the bottom, because it is doing fine.
Tap any row to open that hex on the map. The heading counts the lot, so you can read the state of your realm without reading the list.

Escape closes the Keep and the cell card. It always closed the Guide, History, Character and Codex — the two panels you open most were the two that never got it, so the Keep stayed open behind Research and You with all its buttons still live.
Research says how much wisdom you are short, beside the button. It showed the price and a forecast, and never the plain fact it was refusing on.
Investigate, Light the Altar and temple expansion now say what they are short of too — the last three buttons that greyed out without a reason.

Ward, Consecrate and Expand now say why they are out of reach instead of just going grey. A disabled button with no reason beside it is indistinguishable from a broken one, and a touchscreen has no hover to explain it — so “I press it and nothing happens” was a fair description of what the game was doing.

Ward on ground you have walked for weeks is the worst of them: a hex at full strength cannot be warded any further, and the game answered that by saying nothing at all. It now says so — and when it is timber you are short of, it says that instead.
Consecrate also mentions the other way to pay it: time spent standing in the cell takes the price down.

Fixed the reason nothing seemed to work. The game was stuck in a loop that re-read the entire save about six times a second and got worse the longer you played, so everything else queued behind it: the pouch showed empty while your resources sat in storage, and the build menu — which judges what you can afford from that same reading — refused every building.

The founding gift is exactly one Monument, 60 stone and 10 culture, so the first thing a new player is meant to do was the one thing that could not be done. Your resources now appear as soon as your Hearth is founded, and the Monument can be built.

Revealing ground pays every time now, and says so. Two thirds of the map is plain, plain ground has no resource of its own, and the reveal quietly paid nothing at all on it — so the button really was doing nothing, most of the time. Ground with no resource pays wisdom instead: revealing is looking, and wisdom is what looking gives.
And the payout is visible. A “+N” rises off the pouch with the same colours, words and pling as Collect, instead of the resources appearing in the HUD with no announcement at all.

Better ground is commoner. The old split put three reveals in four on ordinary ground — written for a game where revealing was rare, when it is something you do on every hex you take. Ordinary is still the likeliest single outcome, but no longer most of them.

Fixed a bug that could leave the game stuck on “Listening for the ground beneath you…” forever. A browser is allowed to answer a location request with neither yes nor no, and iPhones do it often — the map waited for an answer that was never coming, and tracking never started either, because it waits for the map. The game sets its own deadline now: if the browser has not answered, the map opens anyway and tracking gets its own try.

A slow phone is no longer called a broken one. A location request that times out means no fix yet — indoors, in a tunnel, on a cold start — and the search is still running, so it says Searching and keeps your last position instead of announcing that your device has no location sensor and throwing the position away.
And when location really is refused, the game says where the switch is. On iPhone it is in two places, and no web page can see or ask about the outer one, so it names both.

The Codex stopped telling you nobody had published when it simply could not ask. Every failure — an endpoint that is not there, a server error, no network — was being reported as an empty world, so publishing your realm and then being told no realm had published was possible. It now says it could not be reached, adds that your own ground is safe on this device, and offers to try again.
And the Codex builds itself the first time it is asked, so a freshly deployed world shows the table straight away instead of waiting for somebody to publish again.

The Codex of Dominion is open — ☰ → Codex of Dominion. Seven measures, and each one shows your figure, your placing, and the best, average and worst across every realm that has published: Land, Ley-line, Consciousness, Population, Works, Provinces and Footfall.

It is a demographics table rather than a scoreboard, on purpose. A ranked list tells six of seven friends that they lost; this tells all seven something true about their own realm, and someone third in Land can find they are first in Ley-line.

Ley-line counts distinct ground walked, not steps taken. A hundred laps of the same block measure one block — the honest answer to how much of the world you have walked, and the only one worth ranking.
Footfall is every day walked on every hex you hold, added up. It is the one measure an afternoon cannot buy: it only grows by coming back.

Mana reaches past your feet now. Farsight reads the ground two rings out from any hex on the map — terrain, owner, all of it — without walking there, so where to put a mine is a decision instead of a guess. It costs 30, and it is the first rite the air school ever had.

Quickening wakes the free ground beside yours at once, one ring around a hex on your border. It costs 120, more than anything else mana buys, and that is deliberate: at six an hour that is twenty hours, and walking the same seven hexes takes ten minutes. It is not a shortcut — it is for ground your feet cannot reach, across water or behind a fence.
It will not take a hex somebody holds, whoever they are. Ground changes hands by siege, over two or three walks on separate days, and no rite gets to skip that.

The opening hint stopped covering the map. It was six lines of centred text floating over the middle of the screen — on the one view whose whole job is showing you where you are — and there was no way to be rid of it until you had done what it said. It is a small card at the edge now, and a tap sends it away until the next thing worth telling you.

It also stopped sitting on top of the map's own buttons. The strip above the status panel already held the attribution toggle and the recenter button, and a full-width panel covered both — two of them were buttons you could see and could not press.

A hex holds one Work. Building used to be a stacking exercise — pile three or four onto your best cell and the rest of the map was scenery. One per hex means the question is which Work this ground should carry, and the answer to "I want another" is to go and walk for more ground.

The cap on how many Works you could hold in total is gone with it. It was six, it counted across your whole realm, and with three hundred hexes claimed every build after the sixth was refused with the word "cell full" — which explained nothing. Land is the only limit now.

Taking someone's ground takes what stands on it. A siege used to raze the building when the cell changed hands; the mine on that mountain is now yours along with the mountain. Build where you can defend.

Saves with crowded hexes are brought forward rather than thrown away: the strongest Work on each stays, everything else comes down, and the full cost of every one is paid back into your pouch — not the half a demolition you chose would return. The map says how many, and the History panel names them.

Feet decide who owns a contested hex. When someone else's Wager claims ground you also hold, the hourly yield used to divide by whoever happened to be stronger the moment their message arrived — a verdict you could not argue with by playing. It divides by the separate days each of you has walked it now. Walk it more, hold more of it.

And the day count is a fact on the card rather than a footnote. "Walked · 12 days" sits with Ground and Yields, and the ownership ring says what the percentage was worked out from instead of just announcing it.

The game tells you what to do next, all the way through the opening. The line above the HUD used to say one thing and then go silent the instant you founded a Hearth — which is exactly when a new player has their first question. It now walks you through four rungs: take the hex beside you, raise a Work on it, spend your wisdom on Research, then go and get ten hexes. Then it stops for good.

It also stopped giving the wrong instruction. The first sentence the game said to anybody was "Walk a closed loop" — a mechanic that has been switched off by default since walking into a hex became the way you take ground.

Research pays now. Until this version a technology unlocked buildings and rites and did nothing whatsoever to what your land produced — the trickle was the same in your first minute and your fiftieth hour. Each technology now lifts the ground it speaks to: Forestry pays on every forest you hold, Mining on every mountain, and the panel says so in as many words.

It is aimed rather than universal on purpose. A bonus that applied to every hex would compound the whole tree into forty times the base yield on a single cell; aimed at its own terrain the best a cell can reach is +16 an hour, and only if you actually own that kind of ground. Which forest-or-mountain realm you are building is now a reason to research one branch before another.

Wisdom now arrives on its own. Every place you hold — your Hearth, and every temple — pays its rate twice an hour: once in mana, which is what Rites cost, and once in wisdom, which is what Research costs. A temple pays six of each now, the same as the Hearth.

Channelling mana into wisdom is gone. It was a button you had to remember to press, twenty-five mana at a time, and it was the only way research moved for anyone without a Library. Research advances by walking and holding ground now, like everything else.

When a Work will not go up, the game now says what to do about it. It used to print the reason in its own words — "That did not go through — at capacity" — which named none of the eight things that can actually stop a build. Each one has a sentence now: what it costs, which research it waits on, or that a Granary is what lets you hold more.

And the limit you were hitting is visible before you hit it. The Build heading shows how many Works you hold against how many you may — that is a limit on you, not on the hex, and nothing on screen had ever mentioned it.

Notices behave like notices. They stack in a column instead of drawing on top of each other — two at once used to mean you only ever saw the second — and each one leaves on its own after a few seconds, or straight away if you tap it. Wave one away and it stays away.

The claim line lets go too. It was written for a closed loop, which happens rarely; now that every hex you walk into reports itself, leaving it up meant the first hex of a walk sat in the HUD until you closed the game. The full record is still in History.

Walking onto new ground finally says so. You get the line — "1 awakened · +10 food" — and the chime, the buzz, the burst of light and the gold flare over the hex you just took. All five were built and none of them had ever fired, because only a closed loop counted as a claim, and closing loops has been switched off by default since the day walking became the way you take ground. The resources were always arriving; the game just never mentioned them.
Each hex now also reports what it paid, so the reward is a number you can see rather than one you have to go and look up in the pouch.

Reload the page and the map opens where you are. It used to insist on a fresh, high-accuracy fix before deciding where to look, time out waiting for one, and open on the fallback in Tampere instead — a minute-old fix is now good enough for that one question. Live tracking still refuses stale fixes, so your ley-line is unaffected.
And if the map does open somewhere else, it now flies to you instead of crawling the whole way at walking zoom.

The map no longer holds you on a leash. Drag it, pinch it, and it stays where you left it — a new button, bottom-right, lights up while the camera is on you and dims once you have looked away. Press it to fly back.
"Here" now does more than open the cell panel: it flies the map back to the hex you are standing in, drops the zoom to walking level, and flashes that hex's edge so you can see exactly where you are.
Map credits moved to the bottom-left corner to make room for the new button.

"Raise your banner" no longer sends you to GitHub. Pressing it now posts your territory straight from the game — one request, no tab, no account — and the Keep tells you it went: "Sent. Others see your realm within the hour." Press it again too soon and it says so.

The shared world is served by its own small service now instead of a scheduled job rebuilding a file in the repo. Nearby realms still appear on your map only with "Share the world" switched on, and your last submission is still kept for a month so you stay on the map without re-publishing.

Share your world. There is a switch in the menu — "Share the world" — off until you turn it on. With it on, other players' realms near you appear on your map, and the Keep grows a "Raise your banner" button: press it and your territory goes out as a GitHub issue that a scheduled job folds into one shared file everyone reads. Your last submission is kept, so you stay on the map without re-publishing every half hour; a realm nobody publishes for a month fades.
Fixed: the founding stash could be handed out twice — a timing quirk in how the accepted Hearth is written through — leaving you with 120 stone instead of 60.
Fixed: accepting a Wager from someone who had built things made it impossible to build anything yourself. Their buildings were counting against your own capacity.
Fixed: a build could take the Work but not charge the pouch. A resource read landing at the wrong moment wrote a stale pouch back over the payment — the other half of the 0.5.41 fix.

No more handouts. The version gift is gone, and so is the safety net that refilled an empty pouch. What you have, you earn: found your Hearth and you are given exactly one Monument's worth of materials to start — 60 stone and 10 culture — and after that, resources come only from taking ground and holding it.

A Collect button. The hourly trickle still fills the pouch on its own, but pressing Collect is when you see it — a small rise of "+N" off the pouch, with how many hours it has been since you last collected. The old automatic hourly jingle is gone; this replaces it, and the "while you were away" card too.
Every time you take a new cell that produces something, it pays — verified now, in a test, for a batch of cells and for taking the same ground twice.

Fixed: building a Work did not cost anything. A resource read that happened to land at the same moment as the spend wrote the pre-spend pool back over it — the always-write introduced in 0.5.40 made that race real. Found by playing a full session against the dev build.

Resources stop jumping on every update. The starter pouch was being handed out again on every version — three times on the 5th alone — which topped every resource back to its floor and buried what your land actually produces. It is a one-time gift now, and a deeper bug it hid is fixed too: a pouch that had never been written had no clock, so the trickle never accrued.
"Empty the pouch" in the menu, with a confirmation. Ground, buildings and research are untouched.
A hex now shows how many separate times you have stood on it — walking away and back counts, standing still does not.
A cell can hold up to three Works now, not one. Build a sawmill beside a storehouse beside a monument.
Every Work draws its own small isometric icon on the map — all of them on a cell, a rival's too. Toggle it off under the menu ("Building icons on the map"); more map filters will follow.
Every owned cell shows an ownership ring now, not only a contested one: a full ring for ground you hold outright, split for ground a Wager also claims.
"Show a rival cell's full detail" toggle — on, you see a rival cell's strength and decay; off, it stays "held by another" and the red ring.

The Guide is a wiki now. Every building, technology and Rite has its own page — what it costs, what it needs, what it does — built from the same tables the game uses, with a live line: how many cells you hold a building on, whether a Rite is yours yet. There is a Reference list of all of them and a search box across the whole book.
The Keep's Mana / Buildings tabs are two big filled pills now — the underline style kept rendering as an invisible dark strip on the dark panel, a third field report of it.
In the build menu, a building's name is now a link to its Guide page. That page lists the cells you have it on, and each one shows it on the map.
Fixed: the name in the You panel would not change — a half-typed name was being wiped on every background re-render before you could commit it.
Fixed: the banner you pick in the Keep now shows on every hex you hold, as an icon. It was a fixed mark that never changed.
Research and rite rows no longer crush their button — "150 wisdom" / "Insight" sit on one line and the description wraps beside them.
Every "+N resource" now shows in that resource's own colour — the same hues as the pouch and the map's yield pips.
A rite you have not researched shows as locked, not a live button, and says which technology unlocks it.

Every temple element now teaches a rite. Fire brings Forgeheart (iron across the domain), water Wellspring (food), nature Greenwake (timber) — the three that used to dead-end on "its rites are still unwritten".
A temple shows the whole path to its rite and every step is researched right there, in order — no more being sent back to the Keep for a prerequisite.
Every technology, rite and Work now carries a one-line description and the concrete thing it gives — "+5 wood / h", "Shelters this cell from decay · 24 h", "Unlocks the Forgeheart rite".

Research has left the Keep. It is a button of its own in the walking bar — ✷ Research, next to Keep and You — and it opens as its own dialog, the way The Wager does. The Keep is Mana and Buildings now.
Rites are still learned at their temple; this is the plain technology tree, in the one place three field reports went looking for it.

The Keep's Mana / Research / Buildings tabs are now right under the header and pinned there — v0.5.35 moved them but they rendered as a thin invisible strip. They're a proper full-width bar now, visible the moment the Keep opens.
The Keep's Mana / Research / Buildings tabs now stay pinned to the top as you scroll, so 'there is no Research tab' stops being true — it was just below the fold.

A temple whose element has a Rite you cannot reach yet names it and the next thing to research in the Keep, instead of a blank 'nothing yet'. And the Keep's Research list, when everything is unaffordable, says where wisdom comes from.

The screen marks the moments it used to let pass: a Consciousness level, a Rite learned, an adventure seen to its end, an achievement earned. Sacred geometry draws itself for under two seconds, and a tap ends it sooner.
It stays a moment, never a decoration — at most four in a minute, and it respects reduced-motion by appearing at once instead of drawing in.

The Wager is a truce now, not a duel. Accepting one puts a friend's whole sanctuary on your map — all of it, wherever it sits — and where their ground meets yours, the cell is shared: still yours, but the hourly yield is split. You can accept the same challenge again any time to refresh it.

A shared cell's detail card shows a small ring — your share against theirs — split by each side's strength when it arrived, or by the days each has walked it when those are equal. Walk it on a new day and you take the whole cell back.
Temples now teach. Choose a temple's element — fire, water, earth, air, nature or spirit — once, and the rites of that element are researched from that temple instead of the Keep.
The Keep's Research list is the plain technologies now; anything that unlocks a rite has moved to its temple, and needs one of that element awake before it can be studied.
A Wager now updates your map the instant you accept it — no more walking a step first to see their ground appear.
Ground that both you and a Wager both claim now shows as a checkerboard of your colour and theirs, instead of looking like ground you hold outright.
Research found a name: the Keep's tech-tree tab was called 'Rites', which read as a ritual, not a way to research new technologies. It's 'Research' now.
Fixed: tapping a technology could take a second or more with no sign anything had happened. The button now shows 'Researching…' immediately.
The status panel is a little more compact now — the resource pouch reflows into two rows instead of three on a fresh sanctuary, when it is holding all nine at once.

Internal: the dev time-machine's day-advance tests are green again — both were checking the wrong thing (your Hearth cell is meant to never decay; a HUD number they read had quietly become the pouch). No player-facing change.
Internal: territory stopped re-reading itself on every tick of the dev clock, which was wasted work outside of testing with the clock.

Fixed: the ley-line could look like it had vanished after a phone-in-pocket stretch. The unwatched-gap marker is now a clearly visible dashed grey line instead of a near-invisible one — the ground you actually walked never left the map either way.
Fixed: choosing a border defence for the Wager right as it opened could silently revert to the default by the time you sealed it.
Fixed: closing the withdraw or delete-progress confirmation from the ☰ menu could drop keyboard focus instead of returning it to the menu.

A new game now opens with a short camera tour: once, right after you accept your Hearth, the view flies out and pauses over each of the six hexes around it, then settles back on you. Drag the map to skip it. It runs once per game.

Fixed: with loop claiming off, a new game opened to an empty map and a blank cell count, and stepping into new hexes took the ground but left the screen unchanged until something else refreshed it. The map now shows the ground you already hold — your Hearth and its ring, or your whole territory on return — from the moment it loads.

Added a browser walkthrough test that starts a new game, walks a line of hexes, and checks the map, the count, the 'New ground' screen, the reveal button, the cell card and map taps — so this path stays covered.

Territory now grows by walking. Step onto an unclaimed hex that touches your ground and it is yours — a 'New ground' screen names it, plays a chime, and offers a button to reveal what it holds (a resource bonus scaled by how rare the site is). Closing a loop to claim the land inside it is now a setting, off by default, in the menu.
Fixed: tapping the map did nothing when you held little or no ground. A tap with no hex drawn under it now selects the hex where it landed.
Fixed: the nation-name field losing its place as you typed. It is isolated from the map's every-second redraw now.

A Wager or shared-world map now carries more than ownership. Each cell brings its terrain and any border building, and the message carries the sender's nation name and flag. Received ground shows as forest, hill or market instead of grey boxes, does not decay on your device, and its detail panel reads 'Held by <nation>, as they saw it 3 days ago'. Accepting a Wager tells you whose ground it is and how many provinces it spans.

Taking a hex now opens like a parcel. Each cell you capture — walked or stolen — sits under opaque gold, and one at a time, rippling out from the middle of the claim, the gold lifts to show the ground underneath while a sacred-geometry sigil bursts off the top. The full-screen summary still follows. Reduced motion keeps the sigils but drops the sweep.

A temple can be consecrated with resources now, not only earned by standing in one cell for ninety minutes. Open a cell you hold and it offers 'Consecrate a temple' for stone and gold — and any time already spent in that cell pays the price down, so a cell walked to often is cheap and one dwelt to the full threshold is free. A consecrated temple draws mana every hour, the same as a revealed one.

Fixed tapping a hex doing nothing — the previous change queried a quest sigil's whole glow, which sat over the surrounding hexes and swallowed their taps, and could throw mid-render besides. Only the sigil itself is a target now, and a missing layer no longer breaks the click.

The Guide fills as you play. Its front page now lists only the topics you have met — the first claim adds Awakening, the first decay adds The Void, and so on — plus the three that are always there because they are the instructions. A new page announces itself with one gold line you can tap.
The Character screen no longer spoils the ladder: it shows the Consciousness levels you have reached, and the next one named but not explained.
The Keep's Mana tab lists your temples now, each with its mana rate and an Expand button — so a temple across the map can be raised without walking to it.
Tapping bare map past your border does nothing now, instead of opening a detail panel for a hex you have never seen. A quest sigil out there still selects its own place.

The Keep is in sections now. A Resources view lists every resource you hold with its per-hour rate, a Collect button that settles the trickle and stamps when you last looked, and the production line. Identity, then Resources, then the Mana / Rites / Buildings tabs, then Realm — what fades, the dark time, the Wager.

Fixed the pouch that would not update. The resource readout was re-reading on every render and cancelling each read before it finished, so only the debug button ever moved the numbers. Now a claim, an hour's trickle and the starter grant all show up as they should.
A new build now reloads itself the moment it reaches your phone, instead of waiting for you to close and reopen the app. Field testers were stuck on stale code.
The starter pouch refills whenever a game with a Hearth is sitting on nothing — not only on a version change. If your resources have been stuck at empty, they will not be after this.
Reverted the fog change: a hex bordering your land shows its terrain again. Only ground you have never come near stays hidden, and that is simply not drawn.

The footer fits again. Four controls (Vigil · Here · Keep · You) and a nine-resource pouch had grown wider than a phone screen, pushing Vigil off the edge — the type in both is smaller now, spacing tighter, and the row wraps rather than clips.

You have a nation. The Keep now opens with its name — yours to set — a banner picked from six hand-drawn presets, and two figures: how many provinces you hold and a rough population. A small gold ◈ flies over ground you hold that carries no building.
A cell's build menu shows only what you can build there right now. The wall of "Wrong ground" rows is behind a "+ N more" tap, and each one names its single blocker — timber, a Rite, or the ground.

A ⌂ Keep button in the footer. The Keep — where mana, Rites and buildings are all run from — used to be reachable only by walking home and tapping its marker. Now it is one tap from anywhere, once you have a Hearth.

An adventure step happens where it happens. You can no longer tap a quest landmark from across the map and take the step — the button only appears while you are standing on that hex, and a stage viewed from afar says "Walk here to take this step". If you open a stage and then walk off, you can still read it, but its choices lock until you walk back.

Standing still no longer scatters your dwell. A stationary phone's GPS wanders the width of a hex, so the cell you were "in" used to flip to a neighbour and back — splitting an hour of waiting across three cells and revealing no place. Now the game holds the cell put while you are still, on the map and in the record, until you actually walk out of it.

Fog of war stops leaking. An unexplored hex no longer shows its terrain on the map — a dim question mark instead — and tapping one now says "Not explored — walk here to see what it holds" rather than opening the full detail panel. Ground you hold, and the hex under your feet, read in full as before.
The pouch shows every resource it holds, not just food, wood, gold and mana. Walk hills and mountains, get stone and iron — and now you can see them. Only the non-zero ones are drawn.

A starter pouch on every new version while the game is in testing: 100 of each material, 30 mana, 30 wisdom, granted once so buildings and research can be tried straight away. It tops up to that floor without shrinking a fuller pouch.

The codex is now a browsable Guide, opened from the menu: a front page grouping every topic, and a How to Play that lays out the whole loop — walk a loop to claim the land inside, walk it again on later days to hold it, ignore it and it rots. Plus a first-walk checklist and a page that translates the game's own words.
Every codex entry has a back link to the Guide and a "See also" list, so a link from the Vigil readout or a History line now opens the whole book, not just one page.
Fixed a black screen on a browser with no WebGL2 (including Chrome's device-emulation mode): the map falls back to the void and the HUD, Guide and History still work.

The Fuming Lake no longer strands you at the statue. The opening step now moves the tale straight to the lake — the walk there is the gate, not a locked choice with nothing to unlock it. The dead-end flavour options are gone.

Ground you have not walked in a while now shows it — a dark blight creeps over the cell, deeper the longer you stay away and worst at the edge of your territory. One walk across it clears the stain. The Hearth never blights.

Something is scattered on the ground. Walk onto the right cell and you find a fragment — a line of a writing, a chord of a seven-pointed star. Seven of them assemble into one inscription in your Character screen. Where they lead comes next.
Starting a game now claims the ring of six cells around your Hearth, not just the one — a home region that usually holds something that produces.
Building marks switched to shapes every font can draw, and the "THE KEEP" label moved down so a building on your Hearth cell is no longer hidden behind it.
The research tab in the Keep is labelled Rites now — that is the tech tree, and it is where you spend wisdom.

Buildings show on the map now — a small mark on the cell, coloured by what it does: green for a Work that produces, gold for knowledge, red for a fortress. A rival's building on your border shows too.

A Character screen, from the ◇ You button in the footer: set your name, read what your Consciousness level actually means, see the items you have found, and a list of achievements with when you earned each.
Come back after a while away and the game shows you what the wait was worth — a card with the resources that accrued, and a chime.
When an hour rolls over mid-walk, a small "+N timber" rises off the pouch with a soft pling.
Fixed the vanishing pouch: an older save whose resource list was shorter now heals itself on load instead of reading as empty.
Dev builds get a "+200 every resource" button in the menu, so a broken run can carry on.
The Fuming Lake begins on the statue's own hex now, not from the Keep — tap the statue and you are in the tale. Each step is an action on the hex it happens at.
Finding an item, and a place revealing itself, now wait for a tap instead of fading on their own — with a sound so you catch them while walking.
A claimed hex throws its yield: "+10 timber" rising off the ground, in the resource's colour.
A new landmark appearing on the map puts a line in the HUD. The History log names what you found.
The Keep has tabs now — Mana, Wisdom, Buildings, Train — where the single Rites line used to be.
Light the Altar (your Anchor Stone) with stone and gold to make more mana an hour, up to three times.
No Library? Channel mana into wisdom at the Altar — a slow trade, but it moves the research along.
The Buildings tab lists every Work with its cost and what it needs; Train is a placeholder for troops later.
The Fuming Lake reveals itself as you go: only the propeller statue at first, then the lake, the hermit, the bridge, the deep — one stop at a time as the story reaches it.
The three ways past the troll are secret. Walk onto the cell where one lies and the game tells you what you found; only then does it appear on your map.
Report a bug or improvement, from the menu: write it or speak it, and it goes to WhatsApp with the build, roughly where you were, and your last few actions attached.
The Fuming Lake's ten landmarks show on the map now — gold sigils with names, so the adventure's "walk to the Wisdom Stone" is somewhere you can actually see.

Adventures: a story with choices, opened from the Hearth. The first is The Fuming Lake — a boy's impossible propeller, a fuming green lake, a hermit who talks to rocks, and a troll doing philosophy on a bridge.
You get past the troll three ways: with a trinket, a weapon, or wisdom — each needs you to have walked to that place and claimed the ground, plus a little to spend.
Every speaker has its own sacred-geometry sigil. It ends the same way every route: cosmically employed.
The History log records each step of an adventure, linked to a new codex entry.
Anomalies show on the map now — a mark on your own ground that changes as you investigate (a site, under study, in a chain).
Investigating an anomaly now costs food, not wisdom — you can do it from a fresh map, before you have a temple.
The ground can hold an anomaly now — strange cells you investigate for a hidden reward, or a short branching story.
A History log of everything you have done, opened from the claim line or the menu. Each entry links to the codex.
A codex: turn Vigil on and a blue link explains it; the log links into ten more entries.
Fog of war — the map only shows the ground you hold and the ring around it, with a small terrain glyph on each.
The Hearth cannot be lost: it never decays and never changes hands.
A hamburger menu at the top holds sound, vibration, Retreat and Delete; the walking bar keeps only Here and Vigil.
A claim plays a chime and a buzz, switchable off. Ground taken from a rival gets a fuller sound.
The Keep opens the nation panel. Härmälä has hand-surveyed terrain around the test area.
Ground two players both hold splits its yield by who has walked it more.
Phase 2.5: the Hearth, adjacency growth, dwell, terrain, warding, and the Wager by hand.
Buildings, a technology tree, mana from temples, spells, and dark times.
Walk a closed loop, claim the land inside it. GPS tracking, the ley-line, loop detection, H3 cells, capture, reinforcement and decay.
